posts.note: Pet-insurance versus UnitedHealth accelerated-TMS bet; the core call is stated twice. Recurring Radial footer ('soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief') logged once as an own-organization claim.
Commentary on the Hultgren et al. meta-analysis; forward-looking items are conditionals about access and cost if adjunctive therapy proves unnecessary. Radial footer logged once.
Commentary on the Mughal/Young et al. meta-analysis; mostly past analysis and normative calls to action ('we need', 'should'). Three hedged items logged.

Satire: a joke PE fund pitch, then a fictional PE-firm ferry-acquisition Q&A. All items flagged sincere=false; the ferry-persona items also own_claim=false. Remaining ferry-fiction lines not logged separately.
LinkedIn retrospective compiled from earlier pieces; almost entirely past metrics. Only general rules of thumb and hedged mechanism claims logged; within-post content promises not logged.

statements.quote: Depression—we have among the most remarkable treatments ever, already here, now, published, and more data are on the way.
statements.context: Opening of the post. The author says accelerated TMS treatments for depression (SAINT at 79% remission; a Brainsway H1-coil six-half-day protocol at 78% remission, top-lined) are already published and that more data are coming.
statements.note: Low-specificity call that further accelerated-TMS data will be published.

statements.quote: However, I’ll put a cash-money bet on your pets getting access to accelerated TMS before your family, at least it comes to UnitedHealth Group’s plans’ coverage.
statements.context: Central bet of the post. Prompted by a Frontiers in Veterinary Medicine RCT of a three-day rTMS protocol for drug-resistant epilepsy in dogs, the author bets that pets will get access to accelerated TMS before UnitedHealth Group plans cover it for humans.
statements.note: Restated later in the post as 'Accelerated TMS for Dogs will be at scale before United covers it.'

statements.quote: I’m calling it now. Accelerated TMS for Dogs will be at scale before United covers it.
statements.context: Restatement of the post's central bet after a list of exotic treatments covered by Trupanion pet insurance: accelerated TMS for dogs reaches scale before UnitedHealth covers accelerated TMS for humans.
statements.note: Restatement of the cash-money bet earlier in the same post. The author adds he would be thrilled to lose.

statements.quote: I think Private Equity will see the goldmine in Accelerated TMS…except…for dogs.
statements.context: After noting private-equity roll-ups of veterinary practices and PE interest in human TMS, the author predicts PE will pursue accelerated TMS for dogs (veterinary), not for humans.
statements.note: Paired with the next sentence about United not budging on human coverage.

statements.quote: Cause despite ample evidence, United ain’t budging any time soon, when it comes to humans.
statements.context: Immediately follows the PE-for-dogs prediction. The author says UnitedHealth Group will not change its coverage stance on accelerated TMS for humans any time soon despite the evidence.
statements.note: Negative call; the author invites United to prove him wrong.

statements.quote: soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief
statements.context: Recurring Radial footer listing treatments offered at Radial, where the author works: Spravato, Nightware, eTNS, PRISM Neurofeedback, 'soon' eCOT-AS by Neurolief, TMS, accelerated TMS and fMRI-guided SAINT TMS. Claim: Radial will soon offer Neurolief's eCOT-AS.
statements.note: Own-organization claim (Radial, Neurolief); boilerplate footer. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: More to the point, if these drugs work on their own, without extra-magic therapy , many more people will be able to access them. It will drive costs down dramatically. It will reduce the need for potentially exploitative training for therapists, which can cost thousands of dollars.
statements.context: Commentary on Hultgren et al. (General Hospital Psychiatry, 2025), a meta-analysis finding therapy hours do not predict psilocybin outcomes. Conditional forecast: if psychedelics work without adjunctive therapy, access expands, costs fall dramatically, and demand for therapist training falls.
statements.note: Compound conditional (access, cost, training demand) premised on 'if these drugs work on their own'.

statements.quote: This problem won’t solve itself overnight.
statements.context: The 'problem' is the lack of diversity in the therapist workforce (about 75% women, 75-85% white; underrepresentation of Black, Hispanic/Latino and male trainees), which the author says makes an equitable new cadre of psychedelic therapists hard to build.
statements.note: Near-truism about a slow-moving workforce trend; logged for recall.

statements.quote: That would mean a more scalable, accessible, and just treatment for many people.
statements.context: Closing of the post. If the mushrooms (psilocybin) themselves are 'the magic' rather than the therapy, the author expects a more scalable, accessible and equitable treatment for many people.
statements.note: Conditional on psilocybin working without adjunctive therapy; restates the earlier access/cost claim.

statements.quote: I would argue that no one loses out if this turns out to be true, other than those in the business of s elling unvalidated training.
statements.context: Follows 'What if the therapy added nothing?' The author claims that if adjunctive therapy adds nothing to psychedelic treatment, the only losers are vendors of unvalidated psychedelic-therapy training.
statements.note: Conditional; the 's elling' spacing is in the source text.

statements.quote: soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief
statements.context: Recurring Radial footer listing treatments offered at Radial, where the author works, including 'soon' eCOT-AS by Neurolief. Claim: Radial will soon offer Neurolief's eCOT-AS.
statements.note: Own-organization claim; same boilerplate footer as in the 2025-08-09 post. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: An important note: I'm highly dubious that, absent a much larger data set, we would see a difference.
statements.context: Commentary on Mughal, Young et al. (JCPP Advances), a meta-analysis of therapeutic interventions after adolescent self-harm (29 RCTs, 3470 participants). The pooled analysis found no difference in mortality; the author expects no mortality difference will be shown without a much larger dataset.
statements.note: Conditional negative call about future evidence on youth mortality after self-harm interventions.

statements.quote: The good news is that we could do these psychotherapeutic things in hospitals, and they might be effective.
statements.context: After stating there is no evidence that medication-focused psychiatric hospitalization saves the lives of youth after self-harm, the author suggests specialized psychotherapies delivered inside hospitals might be effective.
statements.note: Hedged possibility, not a firm call.

statements.quote: They may not want to pay for care that doesn't work, and honestly, I think that's a good idea.
statements.context: 'They' are insurance companies. After urging that insurers pay for specialized self-harm therapies that include families, the author notes insurers may decline to pay for non-specialized care (treatment as usual), which the meta-analysis shows does not reduce self-harm.
statements.note: Borderline: reads partly as a present-tense description of insurer preference; logged for recall.

statements.quote: I have no idea if it will work. However, I can promise you that you will love our fee structure.
statements.context: Joke pitch for 'DoubleDown Health Partners', a value-based-care PE fund the author says he is raising, with a 1% management fee and 10% carry versus the 2-and-20 standard. The author promises prospective LPs will love the fee structure.
statements.note: Satire: the fund is a joke vehicle for criticizing PE fees; the fee critique is sincere, the fund promise is not.

statements.quote: I’ll invest in responsible health things only. I won’t promise the moon. But I’ll take less of your money.
statements.context: Same joke fund pitch. Stated intentions for DoubleDown Health Partners: invest only in responsible health businesses, promise modest returns, charge lower fees.
statements.note: Satirical commitments in the author's own voice; no real fund is being raised.

statements.quote: will require COVID-19 testing. That is a billable medical service. So the ticket will remain $2.75. The copay will be $20, however. And then we bill insurance on top of it.
statements.context: Fictional Q&A in the voice of 'LastChoice BCP', an imagined PE firm that acquired the Hornblower East River ferry and a vampire coven. The persona announces every passenger of the rebranded 'Silent Crossing' ferry will need COVID-19 testing billed to insurance, with a $20 copay on top of the $2.75 fare.
statements.note: Fiction voiced by a PE persona; satirizes PE adding billable medical services. Other ferry-fiction plans (silent horns, venipuncture, pension-funded LBO) not logged separately.

statements.quote: we will also be offering Ketamine Infusions on every voyage, to those who have been thoroughly screened for COVID-19 and Blood-borne pathogens, of course.
statements.context: Closing line of the fictional PE-persona Q&A about the Hornblower ferry acquisition: the persona says ketamine infusions will be offered on every voyage.
statements.note: Fiction voiced by a PE persona; no sincere expectation.

statements.quote: If you write about deeply personal topics about what you're passionate, that's going do well on LinkedIn. ... If you have content that will provoke a conversation, that will do well on LinkedIn.
statements.context: Two items from the author's bulleted 'Takeaways' list in a retrospective on reaching 10,000 LinkedIn followers. Rules of thumb predicting that deeply personal and conversation-provoking posts will perform well on LinkedIn.
statements.confidence_phrase: that's going do well ... that will do well
statements.note: General rules of thumb, not a dated forecast; two adjacent bullets joined with ' ... '.

statements.quote: We can debate, and probably will, the “ construct validity ” of this as a metric
statements.context: Discussing LinkedIn's 2% 'good engagement rate' benchmark and the author's own 7.7% rate. The author expects readers will debate whether engagement rate is a valid metric of success.
statements.note: Trivial forward-looking remark about future discussion; logged for recall.

statements.quote: This is a flaw, albeit an overcomeable one, and how large language models are trained.
statements.context: Section on mentalizing. The author says LLMs are trained on what people wanted to say, not on what people wanted to hear, and calls this a flaw that can be overcome.
statements.note: Implicit hedged call that LLM training can be fixed to model the receiver's mind; borderline.

statements.quote: as the impressions grow, pasture immediate circle of individuals who might have some connection to you, I would imagine it becomes harder to stick some new comment from a new person in a users feed in a way that wakes them up from their slumber, as it were.
statements.context: Explaining engagement per impression as the most difficult LinkedIn metric. The author hypothesizes that as a post's impressions grow past the poster's immediate circle, converting impressions into engagement gets harder.
statements.note: Hedged mechanism hypothesis; 'pasture' is a typo for 'past your' in the source.
